prompt: An order is placed at 19:04:20 and reaches Pub/Sub at 19:08:40. What is its event time?
hint: One of the two times is a fact about the network.

choices.why: Right. The event time is when the order happened.

choices.text: 19:08:40, the moment Pub/Sub received it
choices.why: That is its processing time, the one lesson 21's windows used.

choices.text: The moment the pipeline's window fires
choices.why: A window firing is the pipeline's doing; it is not a time of the order.

choices.text: The difference, 4 minutes and 20 seconds
choices.why: That is the delay between the two times, not either of them.

prompt: Windowed by arrival, Pinheiros shows 95.50 reais between 19:05 and 19:10; by placing time, 80.00. Which is the right answer to "how much did Pinheiros order in those five minutes"?
hint: Ask what each window measured.

choices.text: 95.50, because the money did arrive in that window
choices.why: It arrived then, but `o-504` was ordered at 19:04:20, in the window before.

choices.text: 80.00, the window by placing time
choices.why: Right. The other run answers how much reached Quitanda in those minutes.

choices.text: Neither: windows always change totals
choices.why: Both runs added every order once; only which window held each changed.

choices.text: Their average, 87.75
choices.why: An average of two different questions answers neither of them.

prompt: Why does `late.py` replay the evening through a TestStream instead of publishing it to the Pub/Sub emulator?
hint: Think about what decides the output of each.

choices.text: The DirectRunner cannot read Pub/Sub at all
choices.why: Lesson 21 read Pub/Sub on it; the problem is what decides the result.

choices.text: A TestStream runs much faster than the emulator
choices.why: Speed is not the point; both finish in seconds.

choices.text: Its timing is fixed in the program
choices.why: Right: the arrival order, the clock and the watermark, so each run gives the same output. From Pub/Sub, the result depends on timing nobody controls.

choices.text: Pub/Sub has no way to carry an event time
choices.why: It can, in an attribute read with `timestamp_attribute`; the last section does it.

prompt: Which kind of window is made from the data, per key, rather than known in advance?
hint: One kind closes after a gap.

choices.text: Fixed
choices.why: Fixed windows are aligned to the clock: 19:00 to 19:05 exists before any order.

choices.text: Sliding
choices.why: Sliding windows also start at known times, every period.

choices.text: Sessions
choices.why: Right. A session grows while a key keeps sending and closes after the gap.

choices.text: The global window
choices.why: There is one global window for everything, known before any data.

prompt: Sliding windows of one hour start every minute. In how many windows is each element placed?
hint: Length divided by period.

prompt: `c-02` ordered at 19:02:05 and 19:07:45, and got two sessions with a gap of five minutes. With a gap of six minutes, what would change?
hint: Compare the gap with the distance between the two orders.

choices.text: Nothing: sessions never merge two orders of one customer
choices.why: `c-17`'s first two orders merged into one session with the same five-minute gap.

choices.text: The two orders would be one session, from 19:02:05 to 19:13:45
choices.why: Right. They are 5 minutes 40 seconds apart, under six, and the session ends a gap after the last.

choices.text: Each order would get a session six minutes long, overlapping
choices.why: Overlapping sessions of one key merge; that is how sessions are built.

choices.text: The second order would be dropped as late
choices.why: Nothing here is late: both are in the batch from the start.

prompt: Match each question Quitanda asks to the window that answers it.
hint: One question has no natural clock.

pairs.left: Orders per five minutes, for the evening report
Orders in the last hour, refreshed every minute
What one customer bought in one visit to the app
Orders since midnight, refreshed every minute
pairs.right: The global window with a repeated trigger

right_distractors: Processing-time windows of the publish time

prompt: What does a watermark at 19:06:46 claim?
hint: It is a statement about event time.

choices.text: That it is 19:06:46 on the wall clock
choices.why: The watermark is in event time; on the replay's clock it was 19:07:46.

choices.text: That nothing placed before 19:06:46 is still on its way
choices.why: Right, and it is a guess: `o-504` proved it wrong.

choices.text: That every window ending before 19:06:46 has been written to a sink
choices.why: Windows fire when the watermark passes them; writing to a sink is a later step.

choices.text: That the pipeline is 19 hours behind its input
choices.why: Lag is the gap between the watermark and the present, which this number alone does not give.

prompt: With the default trigger and no allowed lateness, what happens to `o-504` in `late.py`?
hint: Its window had fired before it arrived.

choices.text: It is added to the next window
choices.why: The window is chosen by event time, 19:04:20, and that window is gone.

choices.text: The pipeline stops with an error naming it
choices.why: Nothing reports it; the run ends with a correct-looking table.

choices.text: It is dropped, and nothing says so
choices.why: Right. Pinheiros's first window stays at 128.00 instead of 151.50.

choices.text: It waits until the window fires again
choices.why: The default trigger fires a window once.

prompt: A colleague proposes a watermark ten minutes behind the latest arrival, so that no order of the evening is late. What does that cost?
hint: A window closes when the watermark passes its end.

choices.text: Nothing: the same results, with none dropped
choices.why: The results are complete, but later: that is the cost.

choices.text: Every window comes out about ten minutes later
choices.why: Right, and more state is held meanwhile. The 19:00 window would come out at about 19:15 instead of 19:06.

choices.text: Orders placed in the last ten minutes are dropped
choices.why: A watermark further behind calls less data late, not more.

choices.text: Pub/Sub keeps every message for ten more minutes
choices.why: The watermark is the pipeline's estimate; it changes nothing about the subscription.

prompt: With no allowed lateness, `late.py` dropped `o-504` (23.50), `o-507` (31.00) and `o-510` (8.00). How many reais are missing from its totals?
hint: Add the three.

prompt: With `--lateness 300`, why is `o-507` still dropped?
hint: Allowed lateness is measured against the watermark.

choices.text: Its window's state was gone before it arrived
choices.why: Right: the state went when the watermark reached 19:10. The watermark reached 19:10:16 at 19:11:16; `o-507` came at 19:12:30.

choices.text: `AfterCount(1)` fires only for the first late order
choices.why: It fired for `o-504` and `o-510` both, one pane each.

choices.text: Moema's windows do not accept late data
choices.why: Lateness is a property of the window, the same for every key.

choices.text: Five minutes is counted from when the order was placed
choices.why: It is counted from the end of the window, in watermark time.

prompt: In accumulating mode, Pinheiros's 19:00 window emits 128.00 on time and then 151.50 late. What should a sink that writes one row per window and neighbourhood do with the second pane?
hint: Each accumulating pane is the whole window so far.

choices.text: Add 151.50 to the 128.00 already there
choices.why: That would count `o-502` twice: 151.50 already includes it.

choices.text: Ignore it, because the on-time pane is final
choices.why: The late pane is the corrected total; ignoring it keeps the wrong one.

choices.text: Replace the row with 151.50
choices.why: Right. The last pane is the answer, and replacing is safe to repeat.

choices.text: Write a second row beside the first
choices.why: Two rows for one window and neighbourhood leave a reader to guess which one counts.

prompt: In discarding mode, Moema's 19:00 window printed 45.90, then 9.90, then 0.00 on time. Which consumer reads these panes correctly?
hint: Each discarding pane is only what is new since the last.

choices.text: One that keeps the latest pane per window
choices.why: It would end with 0.00 for a window that holds 55.80.

choices.text: One that keeps the largest pane per window
choices.why: The largest here is 45.90, which misses `o-503`.

choices.text: One that adds every pane of a window
choices.why: Right: 45.90 + 9.90 + 0.00 = 55.80. A pane delivered twice would be counted twice, though.

choices.text: One that keeps only the `ON_TIME` pane
choices.why: That is the 0.00, the empty on-time pane.

prompt: A pane emitted before the watermark reaches the end of its window has the timing ___.
hint: The three timings are printed in capitals by `late.py`.

prompt: What does `ReadFromPubSub(timestamp_attribute='placed')` change?
hint: Without it, the time comes from Pub/Sub.

choices.text: Event times come from the message itself
choices.why: Right, instead of from the publish time. The publisher has to set it, because only the publisher knows when the order was placed.

choices.text: Pub/Sub sorts the messages by `placed` before delivering them
choices.why: Pub/Sub delivers in no such order; the attribute is for the pipeline.

choices.text: Messages without the attribute are rejected by Pub/Sub
choices.why: Pub/Sub does not read attributes; the pipeline does.

choices.text: The window length is taken from the attribute
choices.why: The window is set by `WindowInto`; the attribute only gives the time.

prompt: On the DirectRunner, `from_pubsub.py` kept three orders of ten from 15 October. On Dataflow, with the same ten orders waiting in a fresh subscription, what does the documentation lead you to expect?
hint: Compare where each runner takes its watermark from.

choices.text: The same three orders, because Dataflow also drops old data
choices.why: Dataflow does not compare event times with the wall clock; it estimates from the backlog.

choices.text: An error, because the orders are two weeks old
choices.why: Old event times are not an error anywhere in Beam.

choices.text: All ten in their windows, from the backlog
choices.why: Right: the watermark starts at about the oldest message waiting. Nothing in the backlog is late merely for being old.

choices.text: None, until somebody drains the job
choices.why: Draining fires open windows early; it is not needed for windows to fire.

prompt: Why does a long allowed lateness cost money on Dataflow?
hint: Ask what the runner keeps until a window expires.

choices.text: Each late pane is billed as a separate job
choices.why: Panes are outputs of one job, not jobs.

choices.text: Every window's state is kept until the watermark passes its end plus the lateness
choices.why: Right, and with Streaming Engine that state is part of what is billed.

choices.text: Pub/Sub charges for each message kept beyond its deadline
choices.why: Allowed lateness changes nothing in Pub/Sub; the state is the pipeline's.

choices.text: Dataflow adds one worker per minute of lateness
choices.why: Workers follow the backlog and how busy they are, not a lateness setting.

prompt: Put in order what happens to Pinheiros's 19:00 window in `late.py --lateness 300`.
hint: The watermark moves first; the late order arrives after.
items: `o-502` arrives and goes into the window
The watermark passes 19:05 and the window fires 128.00 on time
`o-504` arrives behind the watermark and the window fires 151.50 late
The watermark passes 19:10 and the window's state is thrown away

prompt: Which of these make a late order count in a fixed window? Choose all that apply.
hint: Some act on the watermark, some on the window.

choices.text: An allowed lateness long enough to cover its delay
choices.why: The window keeps its state, and a late trigger emits the correction.

choices.text: A watermark that lags further behind the arrivals
choices.why: The order is then not late at all, at the price of later results.

choices.text: An early trigger every minute
choices.why: Early panes come before the window ends; they do nothing for data after it.

choices.text: Discarding mode instead of accumulating
choices.why: The mode decides what a pane holds, not whether late data is kept.

prompt: A stream's totals for each night keep coming out a little below the nightly batch over the same events. What is the first thing to suspect?
hint: Lesson 21 made the two comparable on purpose.

choices.text: Late data dropped behind the watermark, past the allowed lateness
choices.why: Right. Dropping makes no noise, and the batch, with every event, shows the gap.

choices.text: The batch counted some orders twice
choices.why: The batch reads each line once; the same transforms run in both.

choices.text: Floating-point rounding in the sum
choices.why: The sums are integer cents until `Format`; rounding would not keep the stream below.

choices.text: Pub/Sub deleted the messages after reading
choices.why: Acknowledged messages are gone from the subscription, but they were counted when read.
